full_text_en:
Shanxi Jiahetai Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. v. Taiyuan Heavy Machinery (Group) Co., Ltd. — dispute over land use rights transfer contract

Ruling Summary

1. Under Article 9 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Disputes over Contracts for the Transfer of State-owned Land Use Rights, where a transferor, without having obtained the certificate for the transfer of state-owned land use rights, concludes a contract with a transferee for the transfer of land use rights, if before the filing of the lawsuit the transferor has already obtained the certificate for the transfer of state-owned land use rights or the people's government with approval authority has approved the transfer, the contract shall be deemed valid.

2. Although China's tax administration laws and regulations clearly specify the taxpayers for the collection of various taxes, they do not prohibit a taxpayer from agreeing with the counterparty to the contract that the counterparty or a third party shall pay the tax, that is, they do not impose mandatory or prohibitive provisions on who actually pays the tax. Therefore, where the parties agree in a contract that a person other than the taxpayer shall bear the taxes and fees for the transfer of land use rights, this does not violate the mandatory provisions of relevant laws and regulations and shall be deemed lawful and valid.

3. Under Article 114 of the Contract Law of the PRC, with respect to the amount of liquidated damages agreed upon by the parties in a contract, only when a party requests an adjustment and the agreed amount of liquidated damages is indeed lower or manifestly excessively higher than the losses caused to the party by the breach of contract may the people's court make an adjustment.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

No. 62, Final (2007) Civil Division 1

Appellant (Defendant at First Instance): Shanxi Jiahetai Real Estate Development Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 10, West First Lane, Bingzhou South Road, Taiyuan City, Shanxi Province.

Legal Representative: Fan Weiming, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Gang, lawyer of Shanxi Yuansheng Law Firm.

Appellant (Plaintiff at First Instance): Taiyuan Heavy Machinery (Group) Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 53, Yuhe Street, Taiyuan City, Shanxi Province.

Legal Representative: Gao Zhijun, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Duan Weiyue, lawyer of Shanxi Dewei Law Firm.

In the case of dispute over a contract for the transfer of land use rights between appellant Shanxi Jiahetai Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Jiahetai Company) and appellant Taiyuan Heavy Machinery (Group) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter Taiyuan Heavy Company), the High People's Court of Shanxi Province rendered Civil Judgment No. 20, First Instance (2006) Shan Min Chu Zi on January 22, 2007. Both parties, dissatisfied with the judgment, appealed to this Court. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and held a hearing in this case on December 18, 2007. Zhang Gang, agent ad litem of Jiahetai Company, and Duan Weiyue, agent ad litem of Taiyuan Heavy Company, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The case is now concluded.

The court of first instance found through trial: On March 26, 2002, Taiyuan Heavy Company (Party A) and Jiahetai Company (Party B) signed an Agreement. The main contents are as follows: … (2) Development parcel: located at No. 48, West First Lane, Bingzhou South Road, Taiyuan City, within the planning area designated by Document No. (2001) 0068 of the Planning Selection Character, approximately 232 meters from north to south, approximately 221 meters from east to west, excluding the boiler room in the southwest corner and existing buildings in the northwest corner, with a reserved space of about 0.5 mu for a transformer station, covering an area of about 64.5 mu. (3) Rights and obligations of the parties: (a) Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be responsible for the demolition and relocation of old houses on the said parcel; (b) Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be responsible for the provision of water, electricity, and road access and leveling of the land, specifically, by June 10, 2002, for the area west of the main road, and by November 30, 2002, for the remaining area; (c) Before the completion of the land transfer procedures, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall assist Jiahetai Company in handling the construction procedures for the project; (d) Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be responsible for the supply of water and electricity during Jiahetai Company's construction, with costs to be paid monthly by Jiahetai Company; the fees for increasing water and electricity capacity and related facilities after the completion of buildings shall be borne by Jiahetai Company; (e) Taiyuan Heavy Company's existing boiler room and transformer station may be used jointly by Jiahetai Company, and the resulting capacity increase fees shall be borne by Jiahetai Company (ownership belongs to Taiyuan Heavy Company); (f) Jiahetai Company shall be responsible for the planning, design, project approval, and other related work and costs required for the development project; (g) Jiahetai Company shall be responsible for the raising, payment, and construction of project costs, as well as the sale of buildings after completion; (h) Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be responsible for handling the land transfer procedures, and the land transfer fees and related transfer costs shall be paid by Jiahetai Company to Taiyuan Heavy Company in accordance with the payment methods and deadlines agreed in the State-owned Land Transfer Contract signed between Taiyuan Heavy Company and the land administration authority, after which Taiyuan Heavy Company shall pay them to the relevant government departments; (i) After the completion of Taiyuan Heavy Company's land transfer procedures and Jiahetai Company's payment of all land compensation fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall then handle the land use rights transfer procedures for Jiahetai Company, with the transfer costs to be borne by Jiahetai Company; (j) Jiahetai Company shall pay Taiyuan Heavy Company land compensation fees of 940,000 yuan per mu (excluding land transfer fees and related taxes) in order to obtain the land use rights; (k) Upon completion, Taiyuan Heavy Company may purchase shops and residential units at prices set by Jiahetai Company on a priority basis; (l) If Taiyuan Heavy Company needs to build staff housing within the community, the land area for such housing shall be deducted from the total area; (m) All types of taxes and fees arising from Jiahetai Company's sale of housing shall be borne by Jiahetai Company. (4) Payment methods: (a) Within two days after the signing of this agreement, Jiahetai Company shall pay Taiyuan Heavy Company 5 million yuan in land compensation fees, and within ten days, pay 15 million yuan; (b) Within ten days after Taiyuan Heavy Company signs the land transfer contract with the land authority, Jiahetai Company shall pay Taiyuan Heavy Company an amount corresponding to the proportion and amount of land transfer fees determined in that contract; (c) After Taiyuan Heavy Company completes the land transfer and has obtained the state-owned land use rights, Taiyuan Heavy Company and Jiahetai Company shall sign a contract for the transfer of such land use rights; within ten days after this contract is approved by the Land Bureau, Jiahetai Company shall pay the remaining land compensation fees; upon receipt of the land compensation fees, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall deliver the land certificate and the approved land use rights transfer agreement to Jiahetai Company for handling the ownership transfer procedures. (5) Liability for breach: (a) Before the completion of the land transfer procedures, if Taiyuan Heavy Company fails to provide water, electricity, and road access and level the land within the time limits specified in Article 3(2) of this agreement, it shall compensate Jiahetai Company for losses caused by work stoppages by paying interest at a daily rate of 0.04% on the amount already paid by Jiahetai Company; if the agreed conditions cannot be fulfilled after more than three months, Jiahetai Company shall have the right to rescind the agreement, and Taiyuan Heavy Company shall refund the amounts received. (b) If Jiahetai Company fails to pay Taiyuan Heavy Company any amount due under Article 4 of this agreement within the time limits specified therein, it shall pay Taiyuan Heavy Company compensation by paying interest at a daily rate of 0.04% on the amount payable; if payment still cannot be made after more than three months from the due date, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall have the right to terminate this agreement, retaining 10% of the amounts already paid as compensation to Taiyuan Heavy Company, and refunding the remainder to Jiahetai Company. (c) During construction, if, due to reasons attributable to Taiyuan Heavy Company, water or electricity supply cannot be guaranteed, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall compensate Jiahetai Company for the direct losses thereby incurred; if Jiahetai Company fails to pay water, electricity, and capacity increase fees as agreed in this agreement, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be exempt from liability. (d) Before the completion of the land transfer procedures, if, due to reasons attributable to Taiyuan Heavy Company, Jiahetai Company is unable to timely complete the examination and approval procedures for the project, thereby affecting construction, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall compensate Jiahetai Company for the direct losses thereby caused; however, if Jiahetai Company fails to pay the relevant fees on time as notified, Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be exempt from liability.

On April 2, 2002, Taiyuan Heavy Company (Party A) and Jiahetai Company (Party B) signed a Supplementary Agreement. The main contents are as follows: (1) In accordance with the time limits of the original agreement, Jiahetai Company shall pay Taiyuan Heavy Company land compensation fees at 940,000 yuan per mu; the turnover tax on the 940,000 yuan/mu shall be borne in the proportion of 76% by Taiyuan Heavy Company and 24% by Jiahetai Company. The 24% turnover tax borne by Jiahetai Company shall be paid simultaneously with each installment of land compensation fees paid by Jiahetai Company under the original Agreement, and any difference shall be settled based on the actual tax paid and the agreed proportion, with any excess refunded and deficiency made up. (2) Except as provided in the preceding clause, all taxes and fees (including but not limited to land appreciation tax, transaction tax, etc.) arising during the performance of the original agreement shall be borne by Jiahetai Company. (3) Any of the above taxes and fees that are required to be paid in the name of Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be paid by Jiahetai Company in full to Taiyuan Heavy Company.

On September 24, 2002, Taiyuan Heavy Company and the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources signed the State-owned Land Use Rights Transfer Contract (hereinafter the Transfer Contract), and Taiyuan Heavy Company obtained the land use rights for the parcel, confirming the transferred land area as 42,968.75 square meters (approximately 64.45 mu).

In December 2002, Taiyuan Heavy Company and Jiahetai Company signed the Taiyuan City Transfer Contract for the Transfer of State-owned Land Use Rights (hereinafter the Transfer Contract for Land Use Rights). The main contents of this contract are as follows: Article 7: The transfer price for the land use rights is 1,223 yuan per square meter, with a total amount of 52,550,800 yuan. Article 8: Taiyuan Heavy Company agrees to pay the land appreciation tax on the transfer to the state in accordance with the original transfer contract. Article 10: Within 15 days of the signing of this contract, Jiahetai Company shall, in accordance with the approval opinion of the Taiyuan Municipal Real Estate Exchange Management Office, handle the relevant procedures and pay the relevant taxes and fees. Article 11: Within 30 days after the signing of this contract, both parties shall apply to the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources for registration of the change in land use rights.

According to Article 4(1) of the Agreement: Within two days after the signing of this agreement, Jiahetai Company shall pay 5 million yuan in land compensation fees; within ten days, it shall pay 15 million yuan in land compensation fees. On April 2, 2002, Jiahetai Company paid 20 million yuan in land compensation fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company by means of a banker's acceptance draft (the draft matured in September 2002).

On October 30, 2002, Jiahetai Company paid 2.5 million yuan in land compensation fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company by check.

According to Article 4(3) of the Agreement: After Taiyuan Heavy Company obtains the state-owned land use rights for transfer, Taiyuan Heavy Company and Jiahetai Company shall sign a contract for the transfer of such land use rights (using the text prescribed by the Land Bureau); within ten days after this contract is approved by the Land Bureau, Jiahetai Company shall pay the remaining land compensation fees. In December 2002, Taiyuan Heavy Company and Jiahetai Company signed the Transfer Contract for Land Use Rights. On January 20, 2003, Jiahetai Company paid 20 million yuan in land compensation fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company by means of a banker's acceptance draft.

On January 5, August 19, August 29, and September 22, 2005, Jiahetai Company paid a total of 3.3 million yuan in land compensation fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company by check and cash.

In summary, Jiahetai Company paid a total of 45.8 million yuan in land compensation fees by banker's acceptance draft, check, and cash, with the balance remaining unpaid.

According to Article 3(8) of the Agreement: Taiyuan Heavy Company shall be responsible for handling the land transfer procedures, and the land transfer fees and related transfer costs shall be paid by Jiahetai Company to Taiyuan Heavy Company in accordance with the payment methods and deadlines agreed in the Transfer Contract signed between Taiyuan Heavy Company and the land administration authority. Article 4(2) of the Agreement: Within ten days after Taiyuan Heavy Company signs the land transfer contract with the land authority, Jiahetai Company shall pay Taiyuan Heavy Company an amount corresponding to the proportion and amount of land transfer fees determined in that contract. On September 24, 2002, Taiyuan Heavy Company and the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources signed the Transfer Contract. On August 12, 2002, Jiahetai Company paid 10 million yuan in land transfer fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company by means of a banker's acceptance draft (the draft matured in February 2003). On September 23, 2002, Jiahetai Company paid 500,000 yuan in land transfer fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company by wire transfer. In total, Jiahetai Company paid 10.5 million yuan in land transfer fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company.

On January 15, 2003, Taiyuan Heavy Company and Jiahetai Company obtained the verification certificate for the transfer of state-owned land use rights. Through the handling of ownership change registration procedures, Jiahetai Company obtained the state-owned land use certificate for the said parcel in January 2003.

In accordance with the provisions on the bearing of taxes and fees in the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement, Jiahetai Company still owes various taxes to Taiyuan Heavy Company.

The court of first instance also found: On December 31, 2002, Jiahetai Company paid 3,867,200 yuan in land transfer fees to the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources.

The court of first instance further found: Taiyuan Heavy Company has paid deed tax of 412,500 yuan; it has declared business tax of 2,812,500 yuan and actually paid business tax of 2,425,260 yuan.

The court of first instance additionally found: The domicile of Jiahetai Company was changed from No. 48, West First Lane, Bingzhou South Road, Taiyuan City, to No. 10, West First Lane, Bingzhou South Road, Taiyuan City.

On January 16, 2006, Taiyuan Heavy Company filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance, alleging that on March 16, 2002 (the correct date appears to be March 26, 2002), Taiyuan Heavy Company and Jiahetai Company signed an Agreement, which clearly stipulated the matters concerning the demolition and compensation for the transfer of the land at No. 48, West First Lane, Bingzhou South Road, Taiyuan City, from Taiyuan Heavy Company to Jiahetai Company. On April 2, 2002, they further signed a Supplementary Agreement, clarifying the issues regarding the bearing of taxes and fees in the Agreement. After the contracts were signed, Taiyuan Heavy Company performed its obligations as agreed, but Jiahetai Company only paid 45.597 million yuan in land compensation fees, still owing Taiyuan Heavy Company a total of 35,486,271 yuan in land compensation fees, related taxes, and fees. Jiahetai Company should pay the arrears and bear liability for its breach of contract in accordance with the contract. The request was for a judgment ordering: Jiahetai Company to immediately pay 35,486,271 yuan in land compensation fees and related taxes and fees, and liquidated damages of 7,558,625.6 yuan (as of January 12, 2006) and liquidated damages until full payment; Jiahetai Company to bear all litigation costs and attorney's fees.

On August 7, 2006, Taiyuan Heavy Company submitted a supplementary complaint to the court of first instance, stating that according to the Transfer Contract for Land Use Rights signed between Taiyuan Heavy Company and Jiahetai Company, Jiahetai Company also owed Taiyuan Heavy Company an additional 52,550,800 yuan in land transfer fees, which had not been paid. Therefore, it added a claim, requesting a judgment ordering Jiahetai Company to immediately pay the land transfer fees of 52,550,800 yuan and bear all litigation costs.

Jiahetai Company argued: Jiahetai Company does not owe any amount to Taiyuan Heavy Company, and Taiyuan Heavy Company's claims should be dismissed. (1) The "land compensation fees" claimed by Taiyuan Heavy Company and the "land transfer fees" are different names for the same piece of land at different stages, and their essence is the land transfer price. On March 26, 2002, when the two parties signed the Agreement, the nature of the land was allocated land, and the agreement was nominally for cooperative development, so the term "compensation fees" was used, but its essence was a contract for the transfer of land use rights. In December 2002, the two parties re-signed the Transfer Contract for Land Use Rights for the same parcel, which was approved by the government. This contract is the final legal document establishing the legal relationship for the transfer of land use rights, with a transfer price of 52,550,800 yuan. Jiahetai Company has overpaid the land transfer fees, and no arrears exist. (2) Jiahetai Company does not owe any taxes or fees to Taiyuan Heavy Company. The Transfer Contract for Land Use Rights does not stipulate that Jiahetai Company shall bear the relevant taxes and fees, and Article 8 of that contract expressly provides that the land appreciation tax shall be borne by Taiyuan Heavy Company. (3) Jiahetai Company does not owe any amount to Taiyuan Heavy Company, and Taiyuan Heavy Company has no right to claim so-called liquidated damages.

The court of first instance held that the main issues in dispute between the parties were: (1) the validity of the Agreement; (2) the validity of the Supplementary Agreement; (3) the validity of the Transfer Contract for Land Use Rights; (4) the determination of the amount paid by Jiahetai Company, the tax issues, and the liquidated damages issue.

(1) Regarding the validity of the Agreement. The court of first instance analyzed the validity of the Agreement from three aspects: 1. The nature of the Agreement. TaiZhong Company argued that the land compensation payment stipulated in the Agreement was used for compensation for on-site housing demolition, employee resettlement, factory relocation, and on-site building compensation, which were two different concepts from the land transfer price stipulated in the Transfer Contract, and could not replace each other. Jiahetai Company argued that the Agreement was, in name, a cooperative development, but in reality, it was a different designation for the transfer of land-use rights at different times; the essence of the Agreement was a land-use right transfer contract. The court of first instance held that the nature of the Agreement was a contract for the transfer of land-use rights. In terms of its content, the Agreement mainly stipulated that Jiahetai Company would pay TaiZhong Company a compensation payment of RMB 940,000 per mu in order to obtain the land-use right of the parcel. It did not have as its basic content the cooperative development based on contributions of land-use rights, capital, etc., for joint investment, joint operation, shared profits, and shared risks. Pursuant to Article 24 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases of Disputes over Contracts Involving State-Owned Land-Use Rights, it should be characterized as a land-use right transfer contract. 2. The relationship among the Agreement, the Supplementary Agreement, and the Transfer Contract. TaiZhong Company argued that the Agreement involved the land's demolition, resettlement, and handling of the transfer procedures; the Supplementary Agreement involved the allocation of taxes and fees; the Transfer Contract was only the transfer of land-use rights. There was no contradiction among the three; the Transfer Contract could not replace the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement. Jiahetai Company argued that the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement were, in essence, land-use right transfer contracts without contractual effect, and were ultimately replaced by the Transfer Contract. The court of first instance held: Formally, the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement were contracts that had not been filed and registered but were held only by the two parties. The Transfer Contract was a contract that had been filed and registered. In terms of content, the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement stipulated a land compensation payment of RMB 940,000 per mu, totaling RMB 60.583 million, with land appreciation tax and related taxes and fees to be borne by Jiahetai Company. The Transfer Contract stipulated a land transfer price of RMB 1,223 per square meter, totaling RMB 52.5508 million, with land appreciation tax to be borne by TaiZhong Company. The clauses on rights, obligations, payment methods, liability for breach of contract, and dispute resolution methods stipulated in the Agreement were not provided for or explained in the Transfer Contract. The two were contracts for the same subject matter but with different forms and different contents. Although both expressed a true intent to transfer, the Agreement was the contract actually performed, while the Transfer Contract was only used for the purpose of completing the transfer registration. 3. The validity of the Agreement. TaiZhong Company argued that the Agreement represented the true intent of both parties, did not violate national laws or regulations, and was a lawful and valid contract. Jiahetai Company argued that the Agreement involved the transfer of allocated land, which violated Article 39 of the Urban Real Estate Administration Law of the People's Republic of China, making it a contract with a validity defect that was replaced by the Transfer Contract. The court of first instance held: The Agreement was a true expression of the intent of both parties and was the contract actually performed in practice. The Agreement and the Transfer Contract were two contracts executed successively for the same subject matter, but the later-executed Transfer Contract did not automatically replace the Agreement, because: First, the Transfer Contract did not abolish the Agreement or the compensation payment clause stipulated in the Agreement, nor did it stipulate that the parts of the Agreement that conflicted with the Transfer Contract were invalid. Second, the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement stipulated contents including demolition, resettlement, performance period, performance method, liability for breach of contract, and dispute resolution methods, whereas the Transfer Contract did not contain the necessary clauses for a contract for such a transaction. Pursuant to Article 78 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, it should be presumed that no change was made. Third, the Agreement did not violate national laws or regulations. When TaiZhong Company and Jiahetai Company signed the Agreement, the land was allocated land. However, during the performance of the contract, after approval by the government administrative department, the right to use the allocated land had been converted into a granted land-use right, and none of the circumstances rendering a contract void under Article 52 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China existed. Pursuant to Article 11 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases of Disputes over Contracts Involving State-Owned Land-Use Rights, the Agreement should be recognized as lawful and valid.

(2) Regarding the validity of the Supplementary Agreement. TaiZhong Company argued that the Supplementary Agreement was lawful and valid. Jiahetai Company argued that the Supplementary Agreement was also a contract with a validity defect and had been replaced by the Transfer Contract. The court of first instance held: The parties, on the basis of the Agreement, signed the Supplementary Agreement, which explicitly stipulated the amounts and methods of payment for land appreciation tax and turnover tax. Its content did not conflict with the Agreement; together with the content of the Agreement, it constituted a complete contract, and the two were identical in nature. Pursuant to Article 61 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, the content of the Supplementary Agreement was a supplement to the content of the Agreement, and it could be confirmed that the Supplementary Agreement had the same legal effect as the Agreement.

(3) Regarding the validity of the Transfer Contract. TaiZhong Company argued that the Transfer Contract was also lawful and valid. Jiahetai Company argued that the Transfer Contract was the only valid contract. The court of first instance held: (1) The land transfer price of RMB 52.5508 million stipulated in Article 7 of the Transfer Contract was the appraised price by the Land Bureau, being the minimum price for indirect regulation and guidance by the state land administration department on the transaction price between the parties to a land transaction, not a representation of a consensus reached by both parties. (2) The price stipulated in the Transfer Contract did not conform to objective facts. According to the Transfer Contract, the price for the land was RMB 52.5508 million, with land appreciation tax to be borne by TaiZhong Company and no stipulation on related taxes and fees, which, according to regulations, would be borne by TaiZhong Company. In that case, when TaiZhong Company received income of RMB 52.5508 million, it would need to pay the state land grant fee of RMB 14.1797 million, land appreciation tax and other related taxes and fees, and also be responsible for demolition and resettlement, and the appraised value of the buildings on the land was RMB 10.412171 million. Clearly, TaiZhong Company's transfer of the land at RMB 52.5508 million was inconsistent with objective facts and the true consensus. (3) In accordance with the price of RMB 52.5508 million stipulated in the Transfer Contract, Jiahetai Company's payment was contrary to common sense. Having already paid RMB 33 million, Jiahetai Company should only have to pay TaiZhong Company RMB 19.5508 million. However, Jiahetai Company paid RMB 20 million on January 20, 2003, and after obtaining the land-use certificate and believing it had overpaid, it made four further payments to TaiZhong Company on January 5, August 19, August 29, and September 22, 2005, totaling RMB 3.3 million, which was clearly inconsistent with common sense. (4) Important clauses stipulated in the Transfer Contract were practically inoperative. Article 8 of the Transfer Contract stipulated: TaiZhong Company agreed to pay the state land appreciation tax in accordance with the original grant contract. However, the original grant contract contained no stipulation regarding the payment of land appreciation tax. (5) The Transfer Contract did not stipulate the delivery of the land, payment of the price, liability for breach of contract, dispute resolution methods, etc., and lacked the necessary clauses for a land-use right transfer contract, which did not conform to general transaction customs. (6) Pursuant to Article 4, Clause 3 of the Agreement: After the land grant procedures for TaiZhong Company are completed and it has obtained the state-owned granted land-use right, it shall sign a land-use right transfer contract with Jiahetai Company (in the form provided by the Land Bureau). Within 10 days after this contract is approved by the Land Bureau, Jiahetai Company shall pay the remaining land compensation payment to TaiZhong Company. After TaiZhong Company receives the land compensation payment, it shall deliver the land-use certificate and the approved land-use right transfer agreement to Jiahetai Company for the completion of the transfer procedures. Article 3, Clause 8 of the Agreement stipulated: The grant fee standard shall be the most favorable price standard that TaiZhong Company can enjoy under the policy. Obviously, the parties had a consensus to reasonably reduce the land transfer fee. From this, it could be inferred that the Transfer Contract was made in accordance with the text stipulated by the Land Bureau for the purpose of fulfilling the approval procedures of the Land Bureau. The parties stipulated the transfer price as RMB 52.5508 million in order to underreport the taxable amount, not to change the originally agreed transfer price. Therefore, the clauses in the Transfer Contract regarding the transfer price and land appreciation tax were not the true expressions of the intent of the parties; such clauses would only reduce the state's tax revenue, and thus such clauses should be deemed invalid. The remaining clauses were substantially similar to the previous agreement, represented the true intent of the parties, and had been reviewed by the land administration department, and the land ownership had been changed through registration; the parties had actually performed them, so they were valid clauses.

(4) Regarding the determination of the amount already paid by Jiahetai Company, the tax issue, and the liquidated damages issue.

(1) The issue of the amount of land compensation payment already paid by Jiahetai Company. TaiZhong Company and Jiahetai Company differed on two points regarding the payments already made: First, the bank acceptance bills. TaiZhong Company argued that the discount interest on the RMB 20 million acceptance bill on April 2, 2002, and the RMB 10 million acceptance bill on August 12, 2002, should be deducted; Jiahetai Company argued that the amount received and the receipted amount should prevail. The court of first instance held: Where the parties did not explicitly agree on the method of payment, Jiahetai Company's payment by bank acceptance bills was not improper, and TaiZhong Company did not raise any objection after receiving the acceptance bills. The claim for deduction of discount interest by TaiZhong Company was not supported. Second, the land grant fee of RMB 3.8672 million paid to the Land and Resources Bureau. Jiahetai Company argued that the grant fee of RMB 3.8672 million it paid to the Land and Resources Bureau should be included in the amount of land compensation payment received by TaiZhong Company. The court of first instance held: TaiZhong Company, in selling the land, actually intended to obtain a land compensation payment of RMB 940,000 per mu, totaling RMB 60.583 million in income, with all other expenses to be borne by Jiahetai Company. Article 3, Clause 9 of the Agreement stipulated: After the land grant procedures of TaiZhong Company are completed and Jiahetai Company has paid all land compensation payments, TaiZhong Company shall handle the land-use right transfer procedures for Jiahetai Company, and the transfer fee shall be borne by Jiahetai Company. Therefore, this grant fee should not be counted in the compensation amount received by TaiZhong Company.

Thus, according to the Agreement, Jiahetai Company should pay TaiZhong Company a land compensation payment of RMB 60.583 million. It had already paid RMB 45.8 million, so it owed TaiZhong Company a land compensation payment of RMB 14.783 million.

(2) The tax issue. The parties stipulated in the Supplementary Agreement: Except for the turnover tax, which was to be borne by TaiZhong Company and Jiahetai Company at a ratio of 76% and 24% respectively, all other taxes and fees were to be borne by Jiahetai Company. Jiahetai Company argued that the taxpayers for the various taxes were clearly defined, and the agreement between the parties was a circumvention of the law and should be invalid. The court of first instance held that the parties' agreement on taxes did not violate mandatory provisions of laws or regulations. The compensation payment paid by Jiahetai Company to TaiZhong Company was the tax-exclusive price agreed upon by the parties; the agreement that various taxes would be borne by Jiahetai Company was lawful and valid. However, TaiZhong Company had not paid the land appreciation tax and stamp duty, and part of the business tax had been paid but not yet occurred. For the taxes and fees not yet paid, TaiZhong Company did not have the right to claim from Jiahetai Company. After each tax or fee actually occurred, TaiZhong Company could claim from Jiahetai Company based on the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement or bring a separate lawsuit. The claim for TaiZhong Company's already paid deed tax of RMB 412,500 was supported.

(3) The liquidated damages issue. The court of first instance held that Jiahetai Company's failure to fully perform its payment obligation was due to the fact that the parties had signed two contracts, and both parties were at fault. Therefore, the request of TaiZhong Company for liquidated damages calculated at a daily rate of 0.04% was not supported. However, since Jiahetai Company's liability for delayed payment was clearly greater than that of TaiZhong Company, its delayed payment objectively caused interest losses to TaiZhong Company. Pursuant to Article 107 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, interest losses are also a form of liability for breach of contract. Although TaiZhong Company did not explicitly request interest losses, it did request liquidated damages. Therefore, Jiahetai Company should bear the interest on the delayed payment.

In summary, the court of first instance, pursuant to Article 64, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Articles 56, 78, 107, and 109 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, ruled: (1) Jiahetai Company shall, within 30 days after the judgment takes effect, pay TaiZhong Company a land compensation payment of RMB 14.783 million and interest thereon (calculated from September 23, 2005, to the date of payment determined by the judgment, based on RMB 14.783 million, at the loan interest rate of the People's Bank of China for the same period). (2) Jiahetai Company shall, within 30 days after the judgment takes effect, pay TaiZhong Company deed tax of RMB 412,500. (3) All other claims of TaiZhong Company were dismissed. The case acceptance fee was RMB 517,998, the preservation fee was RMB 265,000, and other litigation fees were RMB 45,000, with TaiZhong Company bearing RMB 500,000 and Jiahetai Company bearing RMB 327,998.

Jiahetai Company, dissatisfied with the judgment of first instance, appealed to this Court, requesting: 1. that the judgment of first instance be overturned and a new judgment be entered dismissing all claims of TaiZhong Company; 2. that the litigation costs of the first and second instances be borne by TaiZhong Company. The facts and reasons were as follows: (1) Regarding the validity of the Transfer Contract. The Transfer Contract was a true expression of the intent of both parties, complied with legal provisions, was approved by the government, and was the final legal document establishing the legal relationship for the transfer of land-use rights. The land price should be determined according to the Transfer Contract. Jiahetai Company had fully performed its obligations as agreed, and there was no outstanding payment. The first-instance judgment that Jiahetai Company was liable was erroneous. (2) Regarding the validity of the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement. When the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement were signed, the land parcel was administratively allocated land. According to the law, TaiZhong Company had no right to transfer the land parcel, and therefore the Agreement should be invalid. Only after the grant procedures were completed was the validity of the Agreement cured, and it then became legally effective. Although the Agreement became effective, it had inherent defects from the beginning, and it needed to be gradually legalized during the performance process. The Agreement was a preparation for the Transfer Contract and was ultimately replaced by the Transfer Contract. (3) The first-instance judgment found that "the Agreement and the Transfer Contract were two contracts, old and new, for the same subject matter." If so, according to the general principles of contract law, the later contract (the Transfer Contract) should have priority over the earlier contract (the Agreement), and a government-approved contract naturally has priority over an unapproved contract. (4) Where the Transfer Contract and the Agreement contained conflicting stipulations, the Transfer Contract should prevail. Compared with the Agreement, the Transfer Contract changed in terms of scope, area, price, and burden of land appreciation tax; therefore, the Transfer Contract should prevail. (5) The Supplementary Agreement's stipulation on the allocation of taxes and fees violated mandatory provisions of tax law. Even if it was valid, the allocation of the burden of land appreciation tax was manifestly unfair. The taxpayer for land appreciation tax is the transferor, not the transferee, so the Transfer Contract changed the burden of land appreciation tax to be borne by TaiZhong Company. (6) The first-instance judgment incorrectly determined the amount already paid by Jiahetai Company. The grant fee of RMB 3.8672 million paid by Jiahetai Company on behalf of TaiZhong Company should be included in the amount paid. (7) The payment of RMB 3.3 million made after 2005 was forced to induce TaiZhong Company to fulfill its obligation to fully deliver the land; it was an overpayment made under compulsion. (8) Even if the first-instance judgment was correct in its outcome, its allocation of litigation costs violated the People's Court Litigation Fee Collection Measures, exceeding the proportion that Jiahetai Company should bear.

In response to Jiahetai Company's appeal, TaiZhong Company replied: (i) Jiahetai Company's claim that the Transfer Contract replaced the Agreement and the Supplementary Agreement was completely unfounded and a serious distortion of the facts. (ii) Jiahetai Company's objections to the grant fee and taxes agreed in the Agreement were aimed at distorting the agreement and evading debts. (iii) Jiahetai Company's argument that the grant fee of RMB 3.8672 million should be borne by TaiZhong Company was unfounded.

Taiyuan Heavy, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this Court, requesting: (1) to vacate the first-instance judgment and modify the judgment to support all of Taiyuan Heavy's claims in the first instance; (2) to have Jiahetai bear all litigation costs for the first and second instances. The facts and grounds were: (1) The first-instance judgment erred in failing to find that Jiahetai owed land transfer fees. The *Agreement* stipulated that Jiahetai pay land compensation at RMB 940,000 per mu, which was compensation for Taiyuan Heavy's land demolition, resettlement, and provision of utilities, not the land transfer price. The *Transfer Contract* stipulated the land transfer fee, which was the price for the land itself. The provisions of the two contracts did not conflict, let alone overlap, and Jiahetai should fulfill its payment obligations under each contract separately. The contents of the *Agreement* and the *Transfer Contract* were independent, did not overlap, and both bore the seals and signatures of the parties. Under the Contract Law, both contracts were valid and effective. Neither contract contained any clause negating or modifying the other, and they constituted separate rights and obligations of the parties. (2) The first-instance judgment reduced the majority of Jiahetai's liability for breach of contract without basis and was unfair. The first-instance judgment found that Jiahetai was in arrears of land compensation and should perform its payment obligations, but instead of ordering the liquidated damages claimed by Taiyuan Heavy under the contract, it ordered interest at the same-period loan rate, and the starting date for calculating liquidated damages was delayed by as much as two years and eight months, which clearly did not comply with the contract and was unfair to Taiyuan Heavy. Article 4 of the *Agreement* provided that within two days after signing the agreement, Jiahetai shall pay RMB 5 million in land compensation, and within ten days shall pay RMB 15 million; after Taiyuan Heavy obtained the state-owned land use right, the parties shall sign a land use right transfer contract, and within ten days after this contract was approved by the Land Bureau, Jiahetai shall pay the remaining land compensation. Article 5 provided that if Jiahetai failed to pay the amounts due within the time limits specified in Article 4, it shall compensate Taiyuan Heavy by paying interest at the rate of 0.04% per day on the amount due. These provisions were clear and unambiguous, legally binding on both parties, and the people's court should respect the parties' autonomy of will. Under the *Agreement*, Jiahetai should have paid off the land compensation within ten days after approval of the *Transfer Contract*. The parties both agreed that the *Transfer Contract* was approved on January 15, 2003, so Jiahetai's deadline for paying off land compensation was January 25, 2003. Taiyuan Heavy calculated the liquidated damages based on this, and correspondingly deducted several interim payments made by Jiahetai, calculating in segments. As of January 12, 2006, Jiahetai should pay liquidated damages of RMB 7,558,625.6. This calculation was consistent with the contract and the objective facts and should be supported by the court. (3) The first-instance judgment erred in dismissing Taiyuan Heavy's claim for taxes. Paying taxes according to law is an enterprise's obligation; taxes were a necessary expense for Taiyuan Heavy, and Taiyuan Heavy naturally had the right to claim them. Whether the taxes had already been incurred did not affect Jiahetai's obligation to assume them under the contract. Moreover, the calculation of the tax payable was governed by the relevant national laws and regulations. The amount of taxes claimed by Taiyuan Heavy was the result of calculation according to law and had sufficient legal basis, so it should be supported. (4) The first-instance judgment also erred in determining the amount of payments already made by Jiahetai. Among the payments made by Jiahetai, for the RMB 20 million banker's acceptance draft on April 2, 2002, a discount interest of RMB 303,000 should be deducted; for the RMB 10 million banker's acceptance draft on August 12, a discount interest of RMB 156,000 should be deducted.

In response to Taiyuan Heavy's appeal, Jiahetai argued in its defense: Jiahetai did not owe any amount to Taiyuan Heavy, and Taiyuan Heavy's appeal should be dismissed. (A) The *Agreement* and the *Supplemental Agreement* had been superseded by the *Transfer Contract*. Jiahetai had fully performed its payment obligations under the price determined in the *Transfer Contract* and was not in arrears. (B) Jiahetai had fully performed all its payment obligations under the contract and did not owe any amount to Taiyuan Heavy, so Taiyuan Heavy had no right to claim any so-called liquidated damages. (C) Taiyuan Heavy's claim that various taxes and fees, including business tax, deed tax, stamp tax, and land value-added tax, should be borne by Jiahetai was untenable. Because after the *Transfer Contract* superseded the *Agreement* and the *Supplemental Agreement*, the *Transfer Contract* did not stipulate that the above taxes and fees were to be borne by Jiahetai; moreover, Article 8 of the *Transfer Contract* clearly stipulated that value-added tax was to be borne by Taiyuan Heavy. (D) Taiyuan Heavy's assertion that discount interest should be deducted from the payments already made was without basis. When Jiahetai paid by banker's acceptance draft, Taiyuan Heavy issued a receipt for the face amount, thereby acknowledging that no discount interest would be deducted, and now had no right to claim such deduction.

The facts found by this Court in the second instance were the same as those found by the first-instance court.

Opinion of the Court: Jiahetai and Taiyuan Heavy both raised no objection to the authenticity of the *Agreement*, the *Supplemental Agreement*, and the *Transfer Contract*. Considering the parties' appeal requests and the facts and grounds, the issues in dispute in this second instance are: (1) the validity and interrelationship of the *Agreement*, the *Supplemental Agreement*, and the *Transfer Contract*; (2) the amount of land compensation already paid by Jiahetai; (3) whether Taiyuan Heavy's claim for taxes is sustainable; (4) whether Taiyuan Heavy's claim for liquidated damages is sustainable.

(1) Regarding the validity and interrelationship of the *Agreement*, the *Supplemental Agreement*, and the *Transfer Contract*.

First, as to the validity of the *Agreement* and the *Supplemental Agreement*, Taiyuan Heavy argued that the *Agreement* and the *Supplemental Agreement* represented the true intention of the parties, did not violate national laws or regulations, and were legal and valid contracts. Jiahetai argued that when the *Agreement* was signed, the land was allocated land by administrative means; under the law, Taiyuan Heavy had no right to transfer such land, so the *Agreement* was invalid. Further, the *Supplemental Agreement*'s provisions on the allocation of tax burdens violated the mandatory provisions of tax laws. This Court holds: The *Agreement* and the *Supplemental Agreement* were agreements reached by the parties voluntarily through consultation on an equal footing, reflecting their true intention. The *Agreement* not only detailed the area, price, payment method, and liability for breach concerning the transferred land, but also specifically stipulated the rights, obligations, and performance procedures of both parties. At the time of signing the *Agreement*, both Jiahetai and Taiyuan Heavy knew that the land was administratively allocated land, which is why Article 3, paragraph 8 of the *Agreement* provided that Taiyuan Heavy shall be responsible for handling the land grant procedures; and Article 3, paragraph 9 provided that after Taiyuan Heavy completed the land grant procedures, it shall handle the procedures for transferring the land use right to Jiahetai. This contractual conduct did not circumvent the law or harm national interests. In fact, Taiyuan Heavy and Jiahetai completed the transfer of the land precisely in accordance with the above provisions. On September 24, 2002, Taiyuan Heavy signed the *Grant Contract* with Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources, obtaining the right to use the land, and Jiahetai paid the land grant fee; in December of the same year, Taiyuan Heavy and Jiahetai signed the *Transfer Contract*, and Jiahetai paid the land transfer fee to the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources in accordance with the *Agreement*, and subsequently completed the registration of the change in land use right. These were all genuine acts of performing the *Agreement*. Pursuant to Article 9 of the *Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Cases Involving Disputes over Contracts for the Transfer of State-owned Land Use Rights*: "Where a transferor, without having obtained a grant of land use right certificate, enters into a contract with a transferee for the transfer of land use right, but before the action is filed the transferor has already obtained the grant certificate or has obtained the approval of the competent people's government for the transfer, the contract shall be deemed valid." Therefore, the *Agreement* is legal and valid. The *Supplemental Agreement* is a supplemental agreement regarding the tax burdens arising from the transfer of land use right under the *Agreement*, specifying how the taxes and fees for the transfer of land use right are to be borne and by whom. Although China's tax administration laws and regulations clearly specify the taxpayers for various taxes, they do not prohibit taxpayers from agreeing with the counterparty to a contract that the counterparty or a third party shall pay the tax. The provisions of tax laws on tax categories, tax rates, and tax amounts are mandatory, but there are no mandatory or prohibitive provisions on who actually pays the tax. Therefore, the provisions of the *Supplemental Agreement* on the allocation of tax burdens do not violate the provisions of tax administration laws and regulations and are valid. Jiahetai's claim that the *Agreement* was invalid because the transferred land was administratively allocated land and Taiyuan Heavy had no right to transfer it, and that the *Supplemental Agreement*'s provisions on tax burdens violated mandatory provisions of tax laws, is without legal basis and is not supported. The first-instance court's finding that the *Agreement* is legal and valid and that the *Supplemental Agreement* has the same legal effect as the *Agreement* is correct and should be upheld.

Second, as to the validity of the *Transfer Contract*. Jiahetai argued that the *Transfer Contract* reflected the true intention of the parties, complied with legal provisions, and was approved by the government; it was the final legal document establishing the parties' relationship regarding the transfer of land use right, and the price for the transfer of land use right should be as stipulated in the *Transfer Contract*. Taiyuan Heavy argued that the *Transfer Contract* was valid and Jiahetai should bear the obligation to pay the land transfer fee stipulated in the *Transfer Contract*. This Court holds: The reason Taiyuan Heavy and Jiahetai signed the *Transfer Contract* in addition to the *Agreement* was that at the time of signing the *Agreement*, both parties knew the transferred land was administratively allocated land and could not be directly transferred. Only after Taiyuan Heavy completed the land grant procedures and obtained the granted state-owned land use right, could it sign a contract for the transfer of the granted state-owned land use right with Jiahetai, and the parties jointly go through the registration and filing procedures with the land administration authority to complete the transfer of land use right. Therefore, for Taiyuan Heavy and Jiahetai, the *Transfer Contract* was merely for the purpose of going through the registration and filing procedures with the land administration authority to accomplish the transfer of land use right under the *Agreement*, not to change the terms of the *Agreement* or to create new rights and obligations between the parties. For the land administration authority, registration and filing based on the *Transfer Contract* indicated that the land administration authority accepted the price in the *Transfer Contract* and would levy transfer taxes and fees accordingly and handle the relevant procedures. Although the price in the *Transfer Contract* was lower than the price actually agreed upon by the parties, the fact that the land administration authority registered and filed it shows that the authority accepted that the parties could use this minimum price to handle the land use right transfer procedures, and also that this practice of the parties did not violate the relevant regulations of the land administration authority. In fact, the land administration authority handled the change of land ownership based on this *Transfer Contract*. Thus, it can be determined that in this case, the *Transfer Contract* was only used for registration and filing purposes and had no other use; its effect was limited to registration and filing. The *Transfer Contract* neither changed the terms of the *Agreement* nor created new rights and obligations for the contracting parties. An examination of the process and amount of land compensation paid by Jiahetai also shows that after signing the *Transfer Contract*, Jiahetai still paid according to the amount of land compensation stipulated in the *Agreement*. Therefore, Jiahetai's claim that the price in the *Transfer Contract* should be the transfer price of the land use right in this case, and Taiyuan Heavy's claim that it should request additional payment of the land transfer fee based on the *Transfer Contract*, are both inconsistent with the actual circumstances of this case, lack factual basis, and cannot be sustained.

Third, as to the relationship between the *Agreement*, the *Supplemental Agreement*, and the *Transfer Contract*. The parties both agreed that the *Supplemental Agreement* was a supplement to the *Agreement*, but there was significant disagreement between the parties regarding the *Agreement* and the *Transfer Contract*. Jiahetai argued that the *Agreement* had been superseded by the *Transfer Contract*, and the *Transfer Contract* was the only valid contract in this case. Taiyuan Heavy argued that the land compensation stipulated in the *Agreement* was compensation for demolition and resettlement, while the land transfer fee stipulated in the *Transfer Contract* was the price for the land itself; the two contracts did not conflict or overlap, were independent, and were both valid and effective. This Court holds: The purpose of the parties in signing the *Transfer Contract* was to go through the registration and filing procedures for the transfer of land use right. The *Transfer Contract* did not contain any clause providing for the amendment or supersession of the *Agreement*, nor did it establish a new rights-obligations relationship between the parties. Considering the actual performance of the contract by the parties, Taiyuan Heavy's acts of transferring the land use right and receiving land compensation, grant fees, and transfer fees, signing the *Grant Contract* with the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources, and signing the *Transfer Contract* with Jiahetai and registering with the land administration authority, were all acts in performance of the rights and obligations under the *Agreement*. Jiahetai's payment of land compensation, grant fees, and transfer fees, and obtaining the land use right, were also acts in performance of the rights and obligations under the *Agreement*. Therefore, in this case, the *Transfer Contract* was the contract filed for the record with the land administration authority during the land use right transfer procedures, while the *Agreement* was the contract actually performed by the parties. Jiahetai's claim that the *Transfer Contract* superseded the *Agreement* and that the *Transfer Contract* was the only valid contract in this case cannot be sustained. Taiyuan Heavy's claim that the *Agreement* and the *Transfer Contract* are independent and both valid, and that accordingly Jiahetai should pay both land compensation and land transfer fees, also cannot be sustained.

In summary, this Court holds that the *Agreement* and the *Supplemental Agreement* are valid agreements and are the contractual basis for determining the rights, obligations, and liability for breach of contract of the parties.

(2) The amount of land compensation already paid by Jiahetai.

Taiyuan Heavy does not dispute having received a total of RMB 45.8 million in land compensation from Jiahetai in the form of banker's acceptance drafts, checks, and cash. However, it argues that from the RMB 20 million banker's acceptance draft on April 2, 2002, discount interest of RMB 303,000 should be deducted, and from the RMB 10 million banker's acceptance draft on August 12, 2002, discount interest of RMB 156,000 should be deducted. This Court holds: According to Article 4(1) of the *Agreement* signed between Taiyuan Heavy and Jiahetai on March 26, 2002, Jiahetai shall pay land compensation of RMB 20 million within ten days after signing the *Agreement*. Jiahetai should have performed its payment obligation at the agreed time. However, Jiahetai paid this amount of land compensation using a banker's acceptance draft maturing in September 2002, which prevented Taiyuan Heavy from actually receiving the funds at the agreed time. Only by paying discount interest could Taiyuan Heavy obtain the said funds at the agreed time. Jiahetai's act of using a forward banker's acceptance draft to fulfill an obligation due at a fixed time was in effect a delayed payment and constituted improper performance of the contractual obligation. As a result of Jiahetai's improper performance, Taiyuan Heavy incurred a discount interest loss of RMB 303,000, which should be borne by Jiahetai. Taiyuan Heavy's appeal request to deduct this discount interest is sustainable and should be upheld. The first-instance judgment's handling of this issue was improper and should be corrected. As for the RMB 10 million banker's acceptance draft on August 12, 2002, this was payment of the land grant fee by Jiahetai pursuant to Article 3(8) of the *Agreement*. Taiyuan Heavy did not make a claim for the land grant fee in the first instance, so Taiyuan Heavy's appeal request regarding the discount interest on this RMB 10 million banker's acceptance draft is not within the scope of this Court's second-instance review.

Jiahetai argued that the RMB 3,867,200 it paid to the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources on December 31, 2002, as a land grant fee should be counted as part of the land compensation already paid. This Court holds: This sum was paid directly by Jiahetai to the Taiyuan Municipal Bureau of Land and Resources after Taiyuan Heavy and Jiahetai signed the *Transfer Contract* in December 2002. Pursuant to Article 3(9) of the *Agreement*, after Taiyuan Heavy completed the land grant procedures and Jiahetai paid all land compensation, Taiyuan Heavy shall handle the procedures for transferring the land use right to Jiahetai, with the transfer costs to be borne by Jiahetai. Therefore, this sum belongs to the land transfer fee that Jiahetai should bear and should not be counted as part of the land compensation already paid. The first-instance judgment's handling of this issue was appropriate and should be upheld.

In summary, the first-instance judgment's finding that Jiahetai had already paid land compensation of RMB 45.8 million and still owed Taiyuan Heavy RMB 14,783,000 in land compensation was erroneous and should be corrected. The actual amount of land compensation still owed by Jiahetai to Taiyuan Heavy is RMB 15,086,000.

(3) Whether Taiyuan Heavy's claim for taxes is sustainable.

Under the *Supplemental Agreement*, except for the turnover tax, which was to be borne 76% by Taiyuan Heavy and 24% by Jiahetai respectively, all other taxes and fees were to be borne by Jiahetai. As discussed above, the provisions of the *Supplemental Agreement* on the allocation of tax burdens do not violate tax administration laws and regulations; they are valid and effective, and the parties should perform their obligations accordingly. As to whether Taiyuan Heavy has the right to request Jiahetai to pay the taxes it is obliged to bear when Taiyuan Heavy has not yet paid the taxes. This Court holds: The *Supplemental Agreement*'s provisions on the allocation of taxes and fees related to the transfer of land use right merely specify who bears the relevant taxes and fees incurred in the process of transferring the land use right. The *Supplemental Agreement* does not, and cannot, specify when and what kind of taxes and fees are to be paid and in what amounts. Only after the competent authority determines the type and amount of taxes and fees, and Taiyuan Heavy pays them, can Jiahetai then reimburse them. When Taiyuan Heavy has not paid the taxes and no relevant authority has determined the amount of taxes due, its request that Jiahetai pay the taxes for the transfer of land has no factual basis. The first-instance judgment's dismissal of Taiyuan Heavy's claim for reimbursement of taxes not yet paid, while noting that Taiyuan Heavy may bring a separate claim against Jiahetai after actually paying such taxes, was not improper and should be upheld. As for the business tax and deed tax already paid by Taiyuan Heavy, the first-instance judgment's decision to support only Taiyuan Heavy's claim for deed tax but not its claim for business tax was improper and should be corrected. For the business tax of RMB 2,425,260 already paid by Taiyuan Heavy, Jiahetai should bear 24% thereof, i.e., RMB 582,062.4.

(4) Whether Taiyuan Heavy's claim for liquidated damages is sustainable.

**Opinion of the Court**

The Court holds that the *Agreement* clearly defines the specific rights and obligations of the parties, including the time and amount of payment by Jiahetai Company and the liability for breach of contract. Both Taiyuan Heavy Machinery Company and Jiahetai Company shall perform their contractual obligations in good faith and in accordance with the principle of honesty and credit. Taiyuan Heavy Machinery Company fulfilled its obligations by processing the land transfer and assignment procedures and actually delivering the subject plot to Jiahetai Company. Jiahetai Company shall fulfill its payment obligations as agreed, but after obtaining the land use rights, it failed to pay the land compensation fees at the agreed time and in the agreed amount. Jiahetai Company's delay in paying the land compensation fees to Taiyuan Heavy Machinery Company is the main cause of this lawsuit. Therefore, Jiahetai Company's conduct constitutes a breach of contract and shall bear liability for breach of contract as stipulated in the agreement. The judgment of first instance found that Jiahetai Company's delay in payment constituted a breach of contract, but it did not support Taiyuan Heavy Machinery Company's request for liquidated damages calculated at the rate of 0.04% per day as agreed in the contract, and instead adjusted the liquidated damages agreed by the parties at the rate of 0.04% per day to interest calculated at the bank lending rate. Pursuant to Article 114 of the *Contract Law of the People's Republic of China*, a people's court may adjust the amount of liquidated damages agreed upon by the parties in the contract only when a party requests an adjustment and the amount is indeed lower than or excessively higher than the losses caused to the party by the breach. The adjustment of liquidated damages by the court of first instance not only contravenes the agreement between the parties but also lacks legal basis, and shall be corrected. Taiyuan Heavy Machinery Company's appellate claim that Jiahetai Company shall bear liability for breach of contract and pay liquidated damages as stipulated in the agreement is well-founded in reason and evidence and shall be upheld. Since the date of Jiahetai Company's final payment of land compensation fees was September 23, 2005, and Taiyuan Heavy Machinery Company did not previously demand payment of liquidated damages from Jiahetai Company, Jiahetai Company shall bear liability for breach of contract from September 23, 2005.

In conclusion, Jiahetai Company's appellate claims lack factual and legal basis and shall be dismissed. Taiyuan Heavy Machinery Company's appellate claims are partly supported by facts and law and shall be upheld; the remaining part lacks factual and legal basis and shall be dismissed. The judgment of first instance found the facts clearly, but the application of law was partially erroneous and shall be corrected. Pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (2) of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*, it is hereby adjudicated as follows:

1. Affirm Item 3 of the Civil Judgment (2006) Jin Min Chu Zi No. 20 of the Shanxi High People's Court;

2. Amend Item 1 of the Civil Judgment (2006) Jin Min Chu Zi No. 20 of the Shanxi High People's Court to read: Shanxi Jiahetai Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. shall, within thirty days after this judgment takes effect, pay to Taiyuan Heavy Machinery (Group) Co., Ltd. land compensation fees in the amount of RMB 15,086,000, and from September 23, 2005, shall pay liquidated damages calculated at the rate of 0.04% per day on the actual overdue days until the full payment is made;

3. Amend Item 2 of the Civil Judgment (2006) Jin Min Chu Zi No. 20 of the Shanxi High People's Court to read: Shanxi Jiahetai Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. shall, within thirty days after this judgment takes effect, pay to Taiyuan Heavy Machinery (Group) Co., Ltd. business tax in the amount of RMB 582,062.4 and deed tax in the amount of RMB 412,500.

If the monetary payment obligations specified in this judgment are not performed within the period, interest on the debt during the period of delayed performance shall be doubled in accordance with Article 232 of the *Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China*.

Court acceptance fee of first instance: RMB 517,998; preservation fee: RMB 265,000; other litigation fees: RMB 45,000; total: RMB 827,998. Taiyuan Heavy Machinery (Group) Co., Ltd. shall bear RMB 500,000, and Shanxi Jiahetai Real Estate Development Co., Ltd. shall bear RMB 327,998. Court acceptance fee of second instance: RMB 487,998.48, which shall be borne by Shanxi Jiahetai Real Estate Development Co., Ltd.

This judgment is final.
